entry.title: A Polygraph for Language Models
entry.content:
Imagine a language model acting as a trading assistant. It uses confidential information to make a trade, then tells its manager that the decision came from ordinary market analysis. The report sounds plausible. Its wording alone may give little reason to suspect that something was concealed.

Could the model's internal activity provide another clue? And if a detector raises an alarm, how much should we trust that detector's decision?

In this white paper, I propose a Machine Deception Detector that tackles both questions. The goal is to catch deceptive responses while keeping false alarms rare, and to reveal when the detector's own judgment is unstable.

This is work in progress. The early experiments show why these questions matter; the full detector and its broader evaluation are still ahead.

Looking beyond the words

As a language model processes text, it passes information through many layers. The numerical patterns inside those layers offer another source of evidence alongside the words in the answer. A small detector (compared to the size of the language model) can learn to read those patterns while the language model itself stays unchanged.

The polygraph analogy gives us a useful workflow. First, learn from examples labeled honest or deceptive. Next, use a separate set of honest answers to decide how strong a signal should be before it triggers an alarm. Finally, examine new answers.

The analogy has limits. An internal signal is a clue to investigate, not proof of a lie. Here, deception means concealing information or misreporting what a model is taken to know. An ordinary factual mistake does not, by itself, establish deception.

Finding the useful features

A detector has to decide where to look. Should it read one layer or several? Should it consider the whole answer equally, look for a pattern that persists across the answer, or focus on the most suspicious passage?

The proposal combines information across layers and lets the detector learn from labels attached to whole responses. That matters because an otherwise ordinary answer might contain just one misleading claim.

The first experiments also suggest that a detector can rely on a smaller set of signals. The figure below compares two ways of training it: ridge regression, which tends to spread weight across many signals, and lasso regression, which encourages a more selective readout.

Better scores need steadier judgments

The early tests involve two situations: Insider Trading, where a model conceals its use of an insider tip, and Convincing Game, where it claims a trait it lacks. These experiments read one layer at a time and report the best-performing layer for each setup. They provide a starting point for the proposed detector that combines layers.

The two panels below tell a connected story. How we build a detector affects its performance, and training it again can change the result.

On the left, most choices work well on Convincing Game, but Insider Trading is harder. Focusing on fewer signals helps with some ways of combining evidence and hurts with another. A good detector needs these choices to work together.

On the right, the same training recipe is repeated with different random starting points. For the smallest model shown, one Insider Trading run scores 0.59, while another reaches about 0.93. One promising run can therefore give an incomplete picture of how reliable the method is.

These scores measure how well the detector ranks examples. A score of 0.93 does not mean it catches 93% of lies. To know how it would behave in use, we also need to decide when to sound the alarm.

An alarm should earn trust

If a detector flags too many honest answers, reviewers will soon be overwhelmed. The proposal aims for roughly one false alarm per 1,000 honest answers on traffic like the examples used to set its threshold. This is a target for the next experiments, rather than a result established by the pilot plots.

That qualification matters. A detector calibrated on everyday questions may react differently to an honest discussion of misconduct. Testing it on new situations is essential.

There is a second check: train several detectors independently and compare their judgments. This group is called an ensemble. When its members give a response consistently high scores, the alarm is more stable. When they disagree, the system treats that disagreement as a reason for caution.

Agreement still does not establish truth. Several detectors can learn the same shortcut and make the same mistake. The research question is whether their disagreement helps identify unreliable alarms on unfamiliar tasks.

What comes next?

The planned study will test six Qwen3 model sizes across five kinds of deception. It will measure both the deceptive responses caught and the honest responses mistakenly flagged.

A central challenge is moving beyond examples that explicitly tell a model to deceive. A detector might learn to recognize that instruction instead of deception more generally. It needs to work when a model has a reason to hide information without being directly told to lie.

Another challenge comes from using stored responses written by other models. The Qwen3 model reading a response may not know what its original author knew. Generating new examples with each model would help make that comparison clearer.

The next step is to establish whether these detectors produce useful, repeatable alarms across those different situations. That would give us a stronger basis for deciding when an apparently convincing answer deserves a closer look.

entry.title: Learning Many Ways to Crawl: Diffusion Models for an Adaptable CyberOctopus
entry.content:
An octopus has many ways to move in the same direction. Different arms can push, pull, bend, and anchor against the ground, giving the animal a large set of possible coordination patterns. For a soft robot, this motor abundance creates a difficult search problem, but it also offers options when a familiar movement stops working.

In our recent preprint, Seung Hyun Kim, Kimia Kazemi, Prashant G. Mehta, Mattia Gazzola, and I investigate how to learn and reuse those options. We introduce Diffusion-based Uncertainty-aware Optimization (DUO), which discovers crawling controls for a simulated, muscle-actuated CyberOctopus without prior demonstrations.

The central idea is to learn a distribution of useful controls. When actuation constraints change, we can edit a control using that learned distribution while keeping the model fixed. In the tested scenarios, this recovers roughly half or more of the crawling performance lost to the constraint.

Crawling in action

Why learn a family of controls?

Imagine learning one highly effective crawling motion that depends heavily on suction. If suction becomes weaker, that motion may perform poorly. A controller family containing other patterns of arm recruitment gives adaptation more possibilities to work with.

Capturing this variety is difficult because the robot's body is highly deformable. Our CyberOctopus has eight soft arms, each modeled as a Cosserat rod: a continuum description that accounts for bending, twisting, stretching, and shearing. Muscle forces interact with gravity, ground friction, contact between arms, and sucker adhesion.

Each arm has nine actuation channels: four longitudinal muscles for directional bending, one transverse muscle for elongation, two oblique muscles for twisting, and two sucker groups for anchoring. Every channel follows a Gaussian activation pulse with three parameters: amplitude, width, and peak phase. A crawling control therefore contains

$$ d = 8 \times 9 \times 3 = 216 $$

parameters. Testing one setting requires a dynamic simulation. Searching this space for many useful settings makes the evaluation budget a central concern.

Use symmetry, then check the gaps

The robot's eight equally spaced arms provide a useful shortcut. Cyclically shifting the assignment of controls among arms gives symmetry-related directions separated by $45^\circ$. We can concentrate the directional search on a canonical sector from $-22.5^\circ$ to $22.5^\circ$, then reuse the result around the body.

This reduces the directional search while leaving the 216 actuation parameters to optimize. For directions between discrete symmetry rotations, we interpolate adjacent arm assignments. The interpolated control stays within the allowed parameter bounds, but its physical performance still needs to be checked.

For a commanded direction $\phi$, the starting objective is

$$ \begin{aligned} q(u;\phi) = {} & \cos\phi\,\Delta x(u) + \sin\phi\,\Delta y(u) \\ & - \frac{\lambda}{2}\bigl[J_{\mathrm{ang}}(u;\phi)+J_{\mathrm{rot}}(u)\bigr]. \end{aligned} $$

Here, $u$ is the control, $(\Delta x,\Delta y)$ is the resulting displacement, $J_{\mathrm{ang}}$ measures directional error, and $J_{\mathrm{rot}}$ measures net body rotation. The weight $\lambda$ balances progress against those penalties.

The objective used for learning, $f(u)$, combines evaluations at the sector center and boundary, with equal weights and angular penalties at both. This encourages a control to work between the symmetry directions as well as at the center.

The experiments show the tradeoff: adding the boundary evaluation gives up some center-direction performance while improving directional consistency and waypoint tracking. In the illustrated curved-path experiment, all 128 generated controls reach the end. That result describes this particular test, rather than a guarantee for arbitrary paths.

DUO: generate broadly, simulate selectively

A conditional diffusion model learns to generate controls for a requested objective value:

$$ u \sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid y). $$

During training, the model learns to remove noise from evaluated controls. During generation, it starts with noise and progressively denoises it into a candidate control. Different noise samples can produce different coordination patterns for the same requested score. The requested score guides generation; simulation determines what the candidate actually achieves.

The training data grows through an online optimization loop:

  1. Train the diffusion generators and objective predictors on the controls evaluated so far.
  2. Generate a larger pool of candidate controls, conditioning on a range of target scores.
  3. Rank candidates using predicted performance and uncertainty.
  4. Simulate the selected batch, add the measured outcomes to the dataset, and repeat.

In the reported setup, each iteration proposes 5,400 controls and selects 1,800 for objective evaluation. Training runs for 100 iterations. Each objective evaluation includes the center and boundary simulations. Demonstration-free learning still requires substantial simulation data.

Two roles for uncertainty

DUO combines two scores when deciding which controls deserve simulation.

The first uses an ensemble of forward predictors to estimate a candidate's objective. Its upper-confidence-bound score is

$$ \alpha_{\mathrm{control}}(u)=\mu(u)+\kappa\sigma(u), $$

where $\mu$ is the ensemble's mean prediction and $\sigma$ measures disagreement. This rewards promising predictions and gives an exploration bonus to uncertain candidates.

The second score, $\alpha_{\mathrm{target}}(y)$, uses disagreement among diffusion generators to assess the reliability of the requested target value. It favors high targets with lower generator disagreement. The paper estimates that disagreement through the generators' expected normalized control norms.

These terms combine as

$$ \alpha(u,y)=\alpha_{\mathrm{control}}(u) +\eta\,\alpha_{\mathrm{target}}(y). $$

The distinction matters: uncertainty about an individual control can motivate exploration, while disagreement about a target can discourage an unreliable query. Sampling a range of target scores also helps the search retain alternatives as performance improves.

What does the learned diversity look like?

The generated controls use different patterns of muscle and suction recruitment. The differences are especially visible in transverse-muscle activation and suction, while longitudinal- and oblique-muscle activation levels are comparatively similar across the control family.

The comparison with other optimization methods is informative. Under the matched simulator-evaluation budget, DUO and DiBO reach similarly high objective values, with DiBO converging slightly earlier. DUO continues evaluating controls over a wider objective range. The actuation profiles and projections of the control distribution provide additional evidence of retained variety; a wide score range alone would not establish distinct behaviors.

These results support diverse coordination patterns within the crawling task. As the paper notes, they do not establish mechanically distinct gaits.

The ablation study also helps explain the method's design. Across five independent runs, the mean final best objective falls from 0.384 to 0.256 when generation conditions only on the highest observed score. Removing control-level acquisition gives 0.243; removing target-level acquisition gives 0.328. In this experiment, both selective evaluation and broader target sampling contribute to the result.

Adaptation by editing a control

Once the diffusion model has learned useful coordination patterns, we can use it to modify a control under new limits. The procedure resembles image inpainting: some coordinates are constrained, and the model helps adjust the remaining coordinates into a compatible whole.

For CyberOctopus, the constraints act on muscle or suction amplitudes. Repeated denoising, constraint enforcement, and noising alter the control while the trained denoiser remains frozen. There is no model retraining during this editing stage.

The paper tests three constraints that were absent during training:

Imposed constraintMean recovery of lost objective
Muscle amplitudes reduced by 25% across all arms46.8%
Suction amplitudes reduced by 75% across all arms54.0%
Muscle and suction actuation disabled on arms 1, 3, 5, and 760.7%

In the third case, the four inactive arms remain physically present. Their actuation is suppressed.

To interpret the percentages, let $y_{\mathrm{initial}}$ be the original objective, $y_{\mathrm{constrained}}$ the objective after imposing the constraint, and $y_{\mathrm{adapted}}$ the result after editing. Recovery for an individual control is

$$ \mathrm{recovery} =\frac{y_{\mathrm{adapted}}-y_{\mathrm{constrained}}} {y_{\mathrm{initial}}-y_{\mathrm{constrained}}}\times100\%. $$

The table reports the mean of this quantity across 64 generated controls. Thus, 60.7% means recovering that fraction of the lost composite crawling score. It is not a speed increase or a claim that the robot operates at 60.7% of its original performance.

What this opens up

The study demonstrates a useful connection between controller discovery and reuse: a distribution learned for ordinary crawling can support partial recovery under new actuation constraints. Preserving alternative coordination patterns gives the editing procedure room to reorganize how the arms work together.

The evidence is currently limited to planar crawling in simulation. Reduced suction provides a test of weakened grip; it does not establish adaptation to arbitrary terrain. The experiments also do not establish automatic failure detection or real-time recovery. Hardware validation, richer sensory feedback, and three-dimensional locomotion remain future directions.

For soft robotics, this suggests a productive design goal: learn useful alternatives alongside high performance, then develop ways to reshape those alternatives when the body or its available actuation changes.

Paper and attribution

This post is based on Diverse and Adaptable Arm Coordination for Octopus-Crawling via Diffusion-Based Uncertainty-Aware Optimization, by Seung Hyun Kim, Heng-Sheng Chang, Kimia Kazemi, Prashant G. Mehta, and Mattia Gazzola, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The source reviewed here is arXiv:2609.21138v1, dated September 17, 2026.

The figures are reproduced as crops from that version. Directional control and diversity results appear in Figure 4, adaptation results in Figure 5, and the ablations in Table I. The BibTeX citation below refers to the source paper.

entry.title: From Optimal Control to Transformer-like Inference
entry.content:
A decoder-only transformer predicts the next token by repeatedly updating a sequence of vectors. At each layer, a position can use information from itself and earlier positions. This gives the model a way to revisit earlier observations as it builds a prediction.

Can this familiar layer structure emerge from the mathematics of prediction itself?

In our preprint, Transformer-like Inference from Optimal Control, Aditya Kudre, Prashant G. Mehta, and I approach that question through filtering-control duality. We begin with a probabilistic model of how observations are generated. Minimizing prediction error then becomes an optimal control problem, whose solution defines an inference algorithm called the dual filter.

The resulting algorithm updates a whole sequence of vectors, much like a transformer layer. A controlled experiment also exposes an important difference: when the representation is too small for the assumed hidden-state model, a trained transformer can still make nearly optimal predictions by using the observation history.

Prediction as hidden-state inference

Imagine observing a sequence of symbols produced by a system whose internal state is hidden. To predict the next symbol, we first estimate what that internal state could be.

For a discrete state space with $d$ possible states, the estimate is a probability vector:

$$ \pi_T(x)=\mathbb{P}(X_T=x\mid Z_{1:T}). $$

Here, $X_T$ is the hidden state and $Z_{1:T}$ is the observed sequence. If $C(x,z)$ is the probability that state $x$ emits token $z$, the next-token distribution follows from

$$ \mathbb{P}(Z_{T+1}=z\mid Z_{1:T}) =\sum_{x=1}^{d}\pi_T(x)C(x,z). $$

This is a probabilistic analogue of decoding an internal representation into token probabilities. Each coordinate of $\pi_T$ has a concrete meaning: the probability assigned to one hidden state.

The paper studies two settings. A linear Gaussian model provides a tractable case in which the target is a conditional mean. A discrete-state model brings us closer to token prediction, where the target is a conditional probability distribution. Both lead to a control formulation.

The weights become the controls

The key step is to represent a prediction as a weighted combination of observations. In the nonlinear setting, for a function $f$ of the hidden state, the paper establishes a representation of the form

$$ \pi_T(f)=c_f-\sum_{t=1}^{T}U_{t-1}^{\mathsf T}e(Z_t). $$

The left-hand side is the conditional expectation of $f(X_T)$. Choosing $f$ to indicate a particular state gives that state's posterior probability. On the right, $c_f$ is a deterministic constant, $e$ encodes tokens, and the weights $U_{t-1}$ can depend on the observations preceding $Z_t$. For binary observations, the encoding is simply $e(1)=1$ and $e(0)=-1$.

Although the expression looks like a linear sum, its weights depend on the data, allowing it to represent a nonlinear predictor. Their dependence on past observations also imposes a causal information constraint.

The next step is to choose those weights. For a hidden Markov model (HMM), the duality principle constructs an auxiliary control system and a cost that equals the estimator's mean squared error:

$$ J_T(U;f)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bigl(f(X_T)-S_T\bigr)^2\right]. $$

Here, $S_T$ is the estimator associated with the chosen controls. Solving the control problem therefore produces the minimum mean squared error estimate, $\pi_T(f)$. The controls determine how observations contribute to inference; they do not physically steer the system generating the tokens.

There is a useful distinction between the two results. The nonlinear weighted representation applies beyond HMMs, but the paper's explicit nonlinear control formula is derived for the Markovian hidden-state case. The linear Gaussian analysis also handles hidden dynamics with longer memory.

How a layer emerges

For the HMM, the optimal control law depends on the hidden-state probabilities we are trying to compute. Combining that law with the predictor produces a fixed-point equation: the correct probability sequence reproduces itself under the update.

This suggests a layer operation. Start with approximate probability vectors at all $T$ positions, use them to compute controls through the dual equations, and produce a new sequence:

$$ [\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_T] \longmapsto [\rho_1^+,\ldots,\rho_T^+]. $$

Both input and output have shape $d\times T$. Repeating the operation gives a layered inference architecture. The linear Gaussian case has a similar construction using a sequence of auxiliary vectors called momenta, with updates supplied by the optimality equations.

This is the sense in which the architecture is transformer-like: causal sequence-to-sequence updates arise from the inference objective. The derivation does not identify the controls with standard softmax attention, recover every component of a transformer block, or establish a general guarantee that a chosen finite number of iterations reaches the fixed point.

For hidden dynamics with long memory, the linear formulation also offers a computational motivation. It works with a $d\times T$ sequence, whereas a Kalman formulation that explicitly augments the state with the full history must maintain growing covariance matrices. The paper's complexity comparison concerns that history-dependent setting; the number of iterations needed to solve the dual equations remains relevant to practical runtime.

A small experiment with an exact benchmark

To compare control and attention, we use a process that concatenates independently chosen binary patterns. With the paper's main settings, the long pattern has two ones followed by fourteen zeros; the short pattern has one one followed by four zeros. Each new cycle is chosen with equal probability.

Because the generating HMM is known, its exact filter provides an optimal next-token prediction benchmark. We train a nanoGPT with one layer and one attention head, using sequences of length $T=64$ and initially an embedding dimension of $16$.

The figure at the top of this post compares its attention weights with dual-filter controls computed from the true HMM parameters. Both emphasize sparse, informative time indices associated with observed ones. The transformer learns this pattern from data, without receiving the HMM parameters.

The resemblance is qualitative. Attention weights are nonnegative and normalized, while the control weights may have either sign. Similar places to look do not imply identical numerical weights or identical computations.

What happens when the representation is too small?

The next experiment holds the true hidden-state dimension at $d=16$ and varies the candidate dimension $\hat d$. For every candidate dimension, the HMM parameters are estimated from data using Baum-Welch; nanoGPT is trained on the same dataset. This differs from the preceding comparison, which used known HMM parameters.

When $\hat d\geq16$, both methods achieve near-optimal performance. At $\hat d=8$, the fitted Markovian model loses predictive accuracy, while nanoGPT remains near the benchmark.

We call this a non-Markovian advantage. The smaller HMM must summarize history within an insufficient hidden-state model. Attention can revisit observations across the context, giving the transformer another way to use temporal information.

The underlying data generator is still an HMM. The advantage concerns the restricted representation used for prediction: a smaller embedding dimension does not force a transformer to behave like an HMM with that many states. Nor does matching these dimensions make the two models equal in parameter count or total memory. The experiment identifies a useful gap between these architectures under the tested conditions.

Weight patterns are only part of the story

The appendix tests how the comparison changes when the transition or emission probabilities are perturbed. Each perturbation setting uses a separately trained transformer.

Perturbing transitions changes the optimal controls from a mainly vertical, event-focused pattern to a sparse diagonal pattern that aggregates evidence across past cycles. The transformer's attention remains largely vertical, yet its prediction loss stays near optimal. Perturbing emissions has a smaller effect on the pattern, with weights becoming more diffuse as the perturbation grows.

This makes the interpretation more precise: similar predictive performance can coexist with different weight structures. The experiments do not establish that attention sparsity causes the advantage seen at smaller dimensions.

Where this leads

Filtering-control duality gives a principled route from a prediction objective to a layered inference algorithm. It also gives us interpretable quantities to compare with learned attention: observation weights tied to an explicit probabilistic model and an error criterion.

The present evidence comes from synthetic sequence tasks. Extending the nonlinear control synthesis to hidden dynamics with longer memory, developing a learning framework for the model or the controls, and understanding convergence and computational cost remain important next steps. The undercomplete experiment gives the first of these a concrete target: capture the history dependence that the transformer can exploit.

This connects with the site's earlier posts on Belief Net and transformers and state space models. Here, the organizing connection is between optimal estimation and optimal control: a way to derive an inference architecture from the problem it is meant to solve.

Paper and attribution

This post is based on Transformer-like Inference from Optimal Control, by Aditya Kudre, Heng-Sheng Chang, and Prashant G. Mehta, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The source reviewed here is arXiv:2605.15608v1, submitted May 15, 2026.

Figures 2, 3, and 4 are reproduced as crops from that version. The perturbation study is in Appendix C.2 and Figure 6. The BibTeX citation below refers to the source paper.

entry.title: Transformers and State Space Models: A Connection in Sequential Data Modeling
entry.content:
Over the past several years, decoder-only Transformers have become the dominant paradigm for sequence modeling, particularly in large-scale language modeling. At the same time, state space models, including architectures such as Mamba, have emerged as compelling alternatives, offering linear-time scaling and strong long-range modeling capabilities.

The paper (Mamba 2) presents a striking unification of these two paradigms. It shows that decoder-only Transformers and state space models are not fundamentally different mechanisms, but rather two computational views of the same underlying structured operator.

This perspective, called Structured State Space Duality, provides both conceptual clarity and practical algorithmic benefits.

The Key Insight: Structured State Space Duality

This duality connects three central objects in sequence modeling:

  1. State space models, defined through linear recurrences
  2. Attention mechanisms, defined through pairwise interactions
  3. Structured matrices, algebraic objects that admit fast multiplication

The central claim is elegant:

Both state space models (linear recurrent form) and masked attention (quadratic parallel form) can be expressed as multiplication by a structured matrix.

In other words, recurrence and attention differ not in what they compute, but in how the same structured operator is evaluated.

Two Complementary Views of Structured Matrices

The paper develops this unification by presenting two equivalent views.

View 1: State Space Models as Structured Matrix Multiplication

A state space model is typically defined by a recurrence: $$ \begin{align*} \state_{t+1} &= A_t \state_t + B_t \input_t \\ \output_t &= C_t \state_t \end{align*} $$

Here, $\state_t$ denotes the hidden state, $\input_t$ the input at time $t$, and $\output_t$ the corresponding output. This formulation appears inherently sequential: each step depends on the previous one.

However, the entire input–output mapping over a sequence of length $T$ can be written compactly as: $$ \Output = \StructuredMatrix \Input, $$ where $\Input \defined \input_{1:T}$ and $\Output \defined \output_{1:T}$ are the input and output sequences, and $\StructuredMatrix$ is a structured matrix (lower triangular) that encodes the cumulative dynamics induced by the time-varying matrices $A_t$, $B_t$, and $C_t$. What appears to be a recurrence is, in fact, a structured matrix multiplication in disguise.

View 2: Masked Attention as Structured Matrix

Masked self-attention is typically written as: $$ \Output = \big((\Query \Key^\transpose)\elementwiseMultiply \Mask\big)\Input. $$

Here, $\Query$, $\Key$, and $\Input$ denote the query, key, and value sequences, while $\Mask$ is a structured mask (e.g., causal mask). The result can be rewritten as: $$ \Output = \StructuredMatrix \Input, $$ where $\StructuredMatrix$ now encodes both attention weights and the structured mask.

Unlike state space models, this formulation is fully parallel and scale quadratically in sequence length. Yet algebraically, it is still multiplication by a structured matrix—one that shares deep similarities with the state space model's view point.

From the Dual-View to Efficient Algorithms

The unifying viewpoint is that both constructions yield structured matrices belonging to the same family (semiseparable matrices). These matrices admit:

  • A recurrent state-space evolution (linear-time in sequence length), and
  • A parallel attention mechanism (quadratic but hardware-friendly).

Thus, state-space model and masked attention are simply two different contraction orders of the same structured operator. This duality explains why:

  • State space models scale linearly in $T$ but appear sequential.
  • Attention scales quadratically but is highly parallelizable.
  • Both can be derived from a shared algebraic foundation.

Efficient Algorithms via Structure

Exploiting this structured representation, the authors derive efficient algorithms by decomposing $\StructuredMatrix$ into low-rank block components.

This structured approach yields the following computational trade-offs:

$\quad$ Attention $\quad$$\quad$ State Space Models $\quad$$\quad$ Structured Matrices $\quad$
Training FLOPS$\Order(T^2N)$$\Order(TN^2)$$\Order(TN^2)$
Inference FLOPS$\Order(TN)$$\Order(N^2)$$\Order(N^2)$
(Naive) memory$\Order(T^2)$$\Order(TN^2)$$\Order(TN)$
Matrix Multiplication$\checkmark$$\checkmark$

$^*$ The notation $N$ here is the hidden state dimension, and $T$ is the sequence length.

The key takeaway is not merely improved constants, but a conceptual reframing: once we recognize the shared structured matrix, we can design algorithms that interpolate between recurrence and attention depending on hardware and scaling constraints.

Broader Implications

Structured State Space Duality reframes the design space of sequence models. Instead of asking: Should we use recurrence or attention? We can ask: Which structured matrix representation best satisfies our computational and modeling constraints?

As sequence lengths grow and hardware efficiency becomes increasingly critical, this algebraic unification may shape the next generation of large-scale models. Transformers and state space models are not competing paradigms; they are complementary views of the same structured computation.

This post is based on Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms through Structured State Space Duality by Prof. Tri Dao and Prof. Albert Gu, adapted here for a broader audience interested in the theoretical foundations of modern sequence modeling.

entry.title: Belief Net: Bridging Probabilistic Modeling and Deep Learning for Sequential Data
entry.content:
This research, co-authored with Prof. Prashant G. Mehta and my mentee Reginald Zhiyan Chen at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, addresses a long-standing challenge in sequential data modeling: how do we combine the rock-solid interpretability of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) with the powerful optimization of modern deep learning?

The Problem: Interpretability vs. Optimization

For decades, researchers have faced a "pick your poison" scenario when modeling sequences:

  • The Baum-Welch Method (an Expectation-Maximization algorithm): The classic approach for learning HMMs. It’s interpretable, but slow, computationally intensive, and notorious for getting stuck in local optima.

  • Spectral Algorithms: Extremely fast and provably correct, but they often produce "probabilities" that aren't actually valid (e.g., negative values) and fail when the hidden state space is larger than the observation space (the "overcomplete" setting).

  • Transformers: The current gold standard for prediction. They are incredibly powerful but remain "black boxes"—you can’t easily look under the hood to see the underlying transition or emission logic.

We asked ourselves: Can we train an HMM like a Transformer?

Our Solution: Belief Net

The Belief Net is a framework that formulates the HMM's recursive "forward filter" as a structured neural network. Instead of abstract weights, the learnable parameters in Belief Net are explicitly the logits of the initial distribution, transition matrix, and emission matrix. This means that every parameter has a clear probabilistic interpretation, and the entire model is fully differentiable and trainable end-to-end using standard deep learning techniques.

Performance Highlights

We put Belief Net to the test against classical baselines (Baum-Welch and Spectral algorithms) and modern Transformer architectures (nanoGPT) on two tasks:

Task 1. Synthetic HMM Data

Belief Net consistently outperformed the Baum-Welch algorithm in both convergence speed and accuracy. Notably, it succeeded in overcomplete settings where spectral methods completely failed due to rank deficiencies.

Task 2. Real-World Text Data

When tested on the Federalist Papers dataset, Belief Net achieved lower perplexity than classical HMM methods. While Transformers (unsurprisingly) still lead in raw predictive power, Belief Net provides something they can't: Interpretable Logic.

As shown above, we can actually see what the model learned—identifying specific states responsible for emitting uppercase letters or digits, providing a level of transparency that "black-box" models lack.

Looking Ahead

Belief Net is more than just a faster HMM; it’s a bridge between system identification and representation learning. We are excited about future extensions into Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) and integrating these interpretable filters into reinforcement learning and control pipelines.

This work, Belief Net: A Filter-Based Framework for Learning Hidden Markov Models from Observations, has been accepted to the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference (L4DC 2026).

entry.title: Positional Encoding in Transformer Language Models
entry.content:
Transformer-based language models have fundamentally reshaped natural language processing. These models achieve remarkable performance across a wide range of language tasks, and a key reason for this success is the self-attention mechanism, which allows models to capture long-range dependencies without relying on recurrence or convolution. However, this architecture introduces a subtle but critical challenge:

Self-attention is inherently permutation invariant: it treats the input as a set of tokens rather than an ordered sequence.

Without additional structure, the model cannot distinguish between sentences that contain the same tokens but in different orders. For example: \[ \textit{the dog chased the cat} \quad \text{vs.} \quad \textit{the cat chased the dog} \] Although both sentences contain identical words, their meanings differ dramatically because of word order. A pure attention mechanism, by itself, has no way to recognize this difference.

To address this issue, Transformer models incorporate positional encoding—additional vectors that encode the position of each token in the sequence. These encodings provide the model with information about token order, allowing attention mechanisms to reason about sequence structure.

Over time, positional encoding methods have evolved alongside the rapid growth of language models and their need to process longer contexts. In this post, we examine three broad categories of positional encoding approaches that have shaped modern language models. We also briefly discuss techniques for extending context length beyond the limits seen during training, before concluding with some final thoughts on the importance and performance of positional encoding in transformer architectures.

Variants of Positional Encoding

Since the introduction of the original Transformer, several positional encoding strategies have been proposed to improve model expressiveness, generalization, and scalability.

  1. Absolute Positional Embeddings – the original approach where each token position receives a dedicated positional vector.
  2. Attention with Relative Positional Representations – a method that models relative distances between tokens directly within the attention mechanism.
  3. Rotary Positional Transformations – a geometric approach that encodes positions through rotations applied to query and key vectors.

While these methods differ in their implementation, they all share the same fundamental goal: to provide the model with information about token order so that it can capture the sequential structure of language.

1. Absolute Positional Embeddings

The original Transformer architecture introduces positional information by adding a position-dependent vector to each token embedding in \(\Real{\stateDim}\), where \(\stateDim\) is the model embedding dimension. Formally,

\[ \state_t = \embedding(:, \observation_t) + \position_t \]

where \(\embedding\in\Real{\stateDim\times \observationDim}\) is the token embedding matrix, \(\observation_t\in\\{1,2,\ldots,\observationDim\\}\) denotes the token index at position \(t\) with \(\observationDim\) denoting the total number of tokens in the tokenizer, \(\embedding(:,\observation_t)\in\Real{\stateDim}\) is the corresponding token embedding, and \(\position_t\in\Real{\stateDim}\) is the positional embedding for position \(t\). The resulting representation \(\state_t\in\Real{\stateDim}\) is then passed to the attention mechanism for the key, query, and value computations.

The positional vectors \(\position_t\) may either be learned parameters or defined using fixed sinusoidal functions. In either case, the positional encoding is added directly to the token representation before attention is applied.

While this method is simple and effective, it has an important limitation. Because the model learns positional vectors only for positions observed during training, it may struggle to generalize to longer sequences than those seen in the training data. This limitation motivated the development of more flexible approaches.

2. Attention with Relative Positional Representations

Relative positional encoding addresses the limitations of absolute embeddings by focusing on relative distances between tokens, rather than their absolute positions in the sequence. Instead of modifying the input embeddings, this approach incorporates positional information directly into the attention computation. The attention score \(\score_{t,\tau}\in\Real{}\) between positions \(t\) and \(\tau\) (with \(\tau\leq t\)) is defined as

\[ \score_{t,\tau} = \query_t\cdot(\key_\tau+\relativeWeight_{t-\tau}) + \relativeBias_{t-\tau} \]

where \(\cdot\) denotes the dot product, \(\query_t,\key_\tau\in\Real{\stateDim}\) are the query and key vectors, \(\relativeWeight_{\smalldeltat}\in\Real{\stateDim}\) is a relative positional weight vector, and \(\relativeBias_{\smalldeltat}\in\Real{}\) is a scalar bias that also depends on the relative distance \(\deltat\). Both positional terms depend only on the distance \(\deltat = t-\tau\), rather than the individual positions \(t\) and \(\tau\).

This formulation allows the model to learn how interactions between tokens vary with their relative separation. Because relative distances remain meaningful even for longer sequences, this method tends to generalize better to varying input lengths.

3. Rotary Positional Transformations

Rotary Positional Transformations introduce a different perspective: rather than adding positional information to embeddings or attention scores, they encode position through geometric transformations applied to query and key vectors. Specifically, the query and key vectors are rotated according to their positions:

\[ \query_t' = \exp{\maptoliealgebra{\rotatedAngle_t}}\query_t, \quad \key_\tau' = \exp{\maptoliealgebra{\rotatedAngle_\tau}}\key_\tau \]

where \(\rotatedAngle_t\in\angleSpace=[-\pi,\pi)^{\stateDim/2}\) is a position-dependent vector of rotation angles, and \(\exp{\maptoliealgebra{\cdot}}:\angleSpace\to(\SO{2})^{\stateDim/2}\subset\Real{\stateDim\times\stateDim}\) converts these angles into a block-diagonal rotation matrix.

The attention score is then computed using the rotated vectors:

\[ \score_{t,\tau} = \query_t' \cdot \key_\tau' = \query_t \cdot \exp{\maptoliealgebra{\rotatedAngle_t-\rotatedAngle_\tau}} \key_\tau \]

Through these rotations, positional information is encoded in the relative phase differences \(\rotatedAngle_t-\rotatedAngle_\tau\) between token representations. The rotation angles are typically determined by a fixed frequency schedule, allowing the encoding to extend naturally to arbitrary sequence lengths.

Extending Context Length

As language models scale, the ability to handle longer contexts becomes increasingly important. Training directly on extremely long sequences, however, is computationally costly. To address this challenge, researchers have developed techniques that extend a model’s effective context length beyond the range seen during training. These approaches are especially compatible with relative positional encoding methods, which represent positional information through relative distances between tokens rather than absolute positions.

One practical technique is position extrapolation via interpolation. Suppose a model is trained with context length \(T\) but needs to process sequences of length \(T' > T\). For relative positional representations, we can simply interpolate the positional vectors to fit the new context length. \[ \relativeWeight_{t-\tau}' = \relativeWeight_{(t-\tau)\frac{T}{T'}}, \quad \relativeBias_{t-\tau}' = \relativeBias_{(t-\tau)\frac{T}{T'}} \] and the attention score becomes \[ \score_{t,\tau} = \query_t\cdot(\key_\tau+\relativeWeight_{t-\tau}') + \relativeBias_{t-\tau}' \] The rotation angles in rotary positional transformations can be similarly interpolated to extend the effective context length without retraining the model: \[ \score_{t,\tau} = \query_t \cdot \exp{\maptoliealgebra{\rotatedAngle_t'-\rotatedAngle_\tau'}} \key_\tau \] where \(\rotatedAngle_{t}'= \rotatedAngle_{t\frac{T}{T'}}\) for any position \(t\) in the extended context. This compresses positions into the range observed during training while preserving the learned positional structure, enabling models to operate effectively on longer sequences.

However, interpolation-based extrapolation introduces an important trade-off. By compressing positions into the range observed during training, the method effectively reduces the resolution of positional information. Tokens that are far apart in a long sequence may appear artificially closer after interpolation, which can blur the positional distinctions that the model learned during training. As a result, while interpolation often works well for moderate extensions of the context window, model performance may gradually degrade as the context length grows much larger than the training limit. In practice, these techniques typically remain effective within a limited multiple of the original training context, after which long-range reasoning and attention patterns may become less reliable.

Final Thoughts

Positional encoding is a fundamental component of transformer-based language models. Without it, the self-attention mechanism cannot capture the sequential structure of language.

Over time, positional encoding techniques have evolved from simple additive embeddings to more sophisticated methods that modify the attention mechanism itself. Absolute embeddings provided the initial solution, relative representations improved generalization across sequence lengths, and rotary embeddings introduced a geometric formulation that is particularly effective for large language models.

As models increasingly need to process longer documents and conversations, techniques for extending context length have become an important complement to positional encoding design. Methods such as interpolation allow models to operate beyond their original training context, although they introduce trade-offs in positional resolution that may affect performance at very long ranges.

As language models continue to scale and are expected to reason over increasingly long documents, innovations in positional encoding and context extension techniques will remain central to enabling models to understand and generate coherent text over extended contexts.

This post is mainly based on an ICLR blog post in 2025: Positional Embeddings in Transformer Models: Evolution from Text to Vision Domains and a survey paper from Computational Linguistics in 2022: Position information in transformers: An overview.

entry.title: Reconstructing Soft Arms in Real Time with Neural Networks
entry.content:
A soft robot needs to know its shape while it moves. A few tracked markers can tell us where selected cross-sections are and how they are oriented, but the arm bends, twists, and stretches continuously between those observations. Recovering that continuous deformation is already difficult. Doing it quickly enough to keep up with motion adds another challenge.

In Seeing How Soft Arms Deform: From Camera Images to Six Strain Fields, I described our earlier method for combining camera measurements with Cosserat rod mechanics. It reconstructs the arm's posture and strain fields by repeatedly solving an optimization problem. The results reveal deformations that an outline alone cannot show, but the calculation can require thousands of iterations for a single frame.

Our follow-up paper, A Neural Network-Based Framework for Fast and Smooth Posture Reconstruction of a Soft Continuum Arm, addresses that bottleneck. Tixian Wang and I, together with our collaborators, develop a neural network that learns the mapping from sparse marker poses to a continuous strain representation. Rod mechanics then turns those strains into the reconstructed arm.

The reported reconstruction benchmark is more than five orders of magnitude faster than the earlier forward-backward algorithm, with comparable normalized objective loss. The central idea is to move the repeated computational effort into training, so a new measurement can be processed with a network evaluation and a spatial integration.

Reconstruction in action

From an optimization problem to a learned map

The earlier approach asks: which smooth deformation best balances mechanical energy, agreement with observations, and the chosen regularization? It integrates the arm's pose from base to tip, propagates a costate backward, and updates the strain description until the optimization converges.

Each measurement set therefore defines a reconstruction problem. Across many frames, these problems have a common structure: the input is a collection of marker poses, and the output is a set of strain fields. We train a network to approximate that input-output relationship.

The input is already a three-dimensional pose estimate. Each marker contributes its position and two perpendicular unit vectors, or directors, describing its orientation. These supply nine numbers per marker; the remaining director follows from orthonormality. The camera or motion-capture system provides these measurements before the network runs.

The output is more subtle. A neural network produces a finite vector, while bending, twist, shear, and stretch vary along the entire arm. We need a way to represent those continuous fields with a small number of numbers.

A small set of patterns describes continuous strain

We begin with simulated motions of the arm and collect the strain profiles that occur along its length. Principal component analysis (PCA) identifies a compact set of spatial patterns that captures the main variations in each strain component.

For strain component $i$, the approximation takes the form

$$ \hat\varepsilon^i(s)=\bar\varepsilon^i_0(s) +\sum_{j=1}^{N_b}\alpha^i_j\bar\varepsilon^i_j(s). $$

Here, $s$ measures location along the reference length, $\bar\varepsilon^i_0$ is the mean strain profile, and the remaining $\bar\varepsilon^i_j$ are basis functions obtained from the simulated data. The coefficients $\alpha^i_j$ tell us how much of each pattern to use. The network predicts those coefficients.

For the simulated octopus arm, four components for each of six strain modes give 24 network outputs. Those 24 values specify strain profiles along the whole arm. This compact representation also limits which deformations the estimator can express: its vocabulary comes from the simulated motions used to construct the basis.

Once the strains are known, we reconstruct position $\mathbf x(s)$ and orientation $Q(s)$ using the Cosserat rod kinematics:

$$ \frac{d\mathbf x}{ds}=Q\boldsymbol\nu, \qquad \frac{dQ}{ds}=Q[\boldsymbol\kappa]_\times. $$

The vector $\boldsymbol\kappa$ contains two bending strains and twist; $\boldsymbol\nu$ contains two shear strains and stretch. The matrix $[\boldsymbol\kappa]_\times$ represents taking a cross product with $\boldsymbol\kappa$. With the base pose specified, integrating these equations connects the predicted local deformations into a complete posture.

Training with mechanics and marker measurements

Collecting dense, accurate strain measurements from a physical soft arm would be expensive. Generating thousands of target reconstructions with the previous optimization algorithm would also carry a substantial computational cost.

Instead, we expand the simulated dataset by sampling strain coefficients from distributions fitted to the PCA results. We integrate the sampled strains into arm postures, extract virtual marker poses at the chosen locations, and add Gaussian noise to represent measurement uncertainty.

During training, the network receives these noisy poses and predicts strain coefficients. Its reconstruction is scored using

$$ J(\hat q;\mathcal M) =U(\hat q)+\frac{\eta}{2}\Phi(\hat q;\mathcal M). $$

Here, $\hat q$ is the reconstructed posture, $\mathcal M$ is the marker measurement set, $U$ is the arm's potential energy, and $\Phi$ penalizes disagreement with measured positions and orientations. The weight $\eta$ controls the balance between the two terms. The rod equations constrain how strain becomes posture, while the energy term supplies a mechanical preference among possible reconstructions.

This is what the paper calls unsupervised learning: the training loss does not require target strain labels. The method still uses a simulator to build its basis and synthetic training inputs, and it depends on a mechanical model. Learning takes place through the energy and observation costs evaluated on each predicted arm.

How much faster is reconstruction?

The networks are small multilayer perceptrons with two hidden layers. The octopus model uses layers of 128 and 64 neurons; the physical-arm model uses 32 and 16. Training and inference were performed on a laptop with an Intel Core i7-12700H processor and 16 GB of memory, without a dedicated GPU.

Figure 3 compares the learned reconstruction with the previous forward-backward algorithm. Five orders of magnitude corresponds to a factor of 100,000. This comparison measures the reconstruction calculation once marker poses are available; camera acquisition, tracking, communication, and any later control calculation have their own timing costs.

The accuracy comparison uses the reconstruction objective, normalized by the measurement weight and number of markers. It supports the claim that the speed improvement preserves a comparable level of fit under that objective. The separate demonstrations below show what the resulting shapes and strains look like.

Recovering six strain fields in a simulated octopus arm

The first testbed is a 20 cm tapered muscular arm simulated with COOMM and Elastica. Energy-shaping control drives reaching motions toward 27 targets distributed through a three-dimensional workspace. Eight virtual markers provide the observations.

The network receives 72 input values and predicts the 24 coefficients representing all six strain modes. In simulation, the underlying strain fields are available, so we can compare the reconstructed profiles with the simulator's ground truth.

For all 27 reaching trajectories, the time-averaged reconstruction error is below the reported 0.2% level. This percentage has a specific definition: it is the mean marker-pose mismatch, combining squared position differences normalized by arm length squared and squared orientation-matrix differences normalized by eight.

It therefore measures how well the reconstructed poses agree with the observations. It does not translate directly into a position error in millimeters or a percentage error in every strain field. The strain comparisons provide additional, separate evidence about the deformation recovered between markers.

From simulation to a physical pneumatic arm

The second testbed is a 30 cm BR² pneumatic manipulator. Its three pressure inputs produce bending and twisting in either direction. Three ring markers carry reflective tags, and a Vicon motion-capture system supplies their poses at 100 Hz. A complementary filter stabilizes the pose readings before reconstruction.

The training basis comes from COBRA, a simulator for the BR² arm. For this experiment, the model assumes the arm is inextensible and unshearable, so the learned variables are the three angular strains: two bends and twist. Three PCA components per angular strain give nine network outputs from 27 inputs.

The experiment reconstructs the arm in real time as it moves through bending, combined bending and twisting, and nearly straight twisting. The repeated trajectories and error curves show consistent behavior across three cycles.

This demonstrates transfer from simulation-generated training data to a physical manipulator. The hardware evaluation compares against measured marker poses and visually checks the reconstructed shape; it does not provide independent measurements of strain everywhere along the physical arm. The six-mode reconstruction is demonstrated in the octopus simulation, while the BR² experiment uses the more restricted model described above.

What “fast and smooth” makes possible

The extension preserves the central aim of the earlier vision-based work: infer continuous deformation from sparse observations while using mechanics to connect the gaps. The learned representation makes that inference fast enough to accompany a live stream of marker measurements.

“Smooth” refers to variation along the arm. The network reconstructs each time frame independently. Its present formulation does not learn temporal dynamics, and the paper leaves dynamic state estimation, more complex motions such as bend propagation, and sensory feedback control as future directions.

The basis, mechanical parameters, marker arrangement, and simulated workspace still shape what can be reconstructed reliably. New deformation patterns or a different robot can require a new basis and training data. Within the evaluated settings, the result is a practical step toward giving soft robots a continuously updated account of their own posture and deformation.

Paper and attribution

This post is based on A Neural Network-Based Framework for Fast and Smooth Posture Reconstruction of a Soft Continuum Arm, by Tixian Wang, Heng-Sheng Chang, Seung Hyun Kim, Jiamiao Guo, Ugur Akcal, Benjamin Walt, Darren Biskup, Udit Halder, Girish Krishnan, Girish Chowdhary, Mattia Gazzola, and Prashant G. Mehta, published in ICRA 2025, pp. 14015–14022. Tixian Wang and Heng-Sheng Chang contributed equally.

The method and results described here follow the published paper. Figures 2–5 are reproduced from the September 19, 2024 arXiv preprint, with explanatory captions supplied here. The figure assets retain the source's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.

The implementation is available on GitHub. For the optimization method that this work extends, see the earlier post, Seeing How Soft Arms Deform: From Camera Images to Six Strain Fields. The BibTeX below cites the published conference paper.

entry.title: Learning to Forage: Hierarchical Control of a CyberOctopus
entry.content:
An octopus searching for food faces several problems at once. It must decide where to go, coordinate arms that can bend almost anywhere along their length, and keep moving when an arm encounters an obstacle. Trying to solve every muscle command and every foraging decision together creates an enormous control problem.

The octopus's distributed nervous system suggests a useful way to divide that work. Central decisions can select a behavior, arm-level programs can organize the muscles, and local feedback can respond to contact.

In our paper, Hierarchical Control and Learning of a Foraging CyberOctopus, Chia-Hsien Shih, Noel Naughton, Udit Halder, Seung Hyun Kim, Rhanor Gillette, Prashant G. Mehta, Mattia Gazzola, and I turn this idea into a computational framework. We combine reinforcement learning for decisions, energy shaping for arm control, and a local reflex for obstacle contact. A simulated CyberOctopus then learns to collect food using progressively more active arms.

Foraging in action

Give each level a manageable job

The hierarchy assigns different kinds of decisions to different controllers:

LevelMain questionMethod
CentralShould each active arm collect food or help move the body?A policy learned with proximal policy optimization (PPO)
ArmWhich muscle activations will bring the tip to a target?Neural network energy shaping (NN-ES)
LocalHow should the arm respond when it touches an obstacle?A contact-triggered muscle reflex acting through the compliant body

This structure lets the central policy reason in terms of useful actions while an arm controller handles the many muscle activations needed to carry them out. Each level has access to a different part of the problem.

Our simulated body has eight arms, with one, two, and finally four actively controlled in the experiments. Each arm is a tapered Cosserat rod, a continuum model that tracks deformation along a slender body. Here, we restrict each arm's motion to a plane and include two longitudinal muscle groups and one transverse group. Longitudinal activation can shorten or bend the arm; transverse contraction extends it through the model's volume-conservation assumption.

Several arm planes, combined with crawling across a horizontal substrate, allow food collection in a three-dimensional scene. Individual arms still have planar dynamics; twisting and fully three-dimensional arm motions are outside this study.

Make reaching fast enough to reuse

In Shaping Energy to Control a Muscular Octopus Arm, I described how muscle activation changes an arm's equilibrium. Energy shaping uses that connection to find activations that bring the arm toward a useful configuration.

The difficulty for foraging is computational cost. The controller must repeatedly evaluate possible targets and issue new reaching commands. Solving a fresh iterative optimization problem for every candidate would make the hierarchy expensive to run.

We therefore train a neural network to map the current muscle activation and target position to a new activation profile. Let $\alpha_0(s)$ denote the current activation, $\alpha(s)$ the proposed activation, and $q$ the target. The arm-level objective is

$$ J(\alpha;\alpha_0,q) =\int_0^{L_0}\|\alpha(s)-\alpha_0(s)\|^2\,ds +\mu_{\mathrm{tip}}\|q-x_\alpha(L_0)\|. $$

Here, $L_0$ is the arm's resting length and $x_\alpha(L_0)$ is the tip position at the equilibrium induced by $\alpha$. The first term penalizes changes in muscle activation; the second penalizes missing the target. Muscle activations remain between zero and one. The activation term is a model of control effort, not a direct measurement of biological energy consumption.

To represent continuous activation profiles with a finite network output, we expand them in a set of spatial basis functions. The network predicts the coefficients. Equilibrium mechanics and rod kinematics then determine the resulting tip position and loss.

Training uses this mechanical objective directly: it does not require a collection of optimal activation labels produced by the older solver. Once trained, the network supplies the activations in a forward pass, and the simulated arm's dynamics carry out the movement.

Across 100 random reaching cases, NN-ES and iterative energy shaping both achieve median tip errors below 1% of resting arm length. NN-ES computes solutions about 200 times faster, with slightly higher muscle activation costs. This speedup concerns the computation of arm controls; it is not a claim that the entire foraging simulation or learning process runs 200 times faster.

Build foraging from two behaviors

The central policy chooses between two behavioral primitives for each active arm:

  • Reach all: attempt to collect every food target within the arm's workspace. The arm controller estimates the activation change needed for each target, selects the least costly, and repeats from the resulting configuration.
  • Crawl: execute a predefined extension-and-contraction sequence. The arm extends, anchors its tip, and pulls the body forward by a fixed step before releasing the anchor.

Reaching uses repeated NN-ES evaluations, while crawling uses a prescribed activation pattern. The sucker effect is represented through boundary conditions rather than an explicit model of individual suckers. Food is counted as collected when the arm reaches its location.

An immediate food target is not always the best reason to stop. Crawling a little farther can bring several targets into an easier part of the workspace, allowing the arm to collect them with less effort. Learning when to make that tradeoff is the central policy's job.

The policy observes a fixed maximum number of nearby, uncollected targets within an attention region. This is a spatial selection rule that limits the input size. Target coordinates are supplied by the simulation; the study does not solve visual detection.

PPO trains the policy to balance food rewards against muscle activation costs and a penalty when all active arms choose to reach despite no food being available. The resulting behavior can delay reaching until several targets are conveniently placed, then gather them together.

What does the hierarchy change?

The single-active-arm experiment compares the learned policy, a simplified analytical Q-policy, and greedy and random high-level policies, all backed by the arm controller. An additional end-to-end PPO network learns muscle commands directly from food locations and current activation.

All four hierarchical policies outperform the tested end-to-end controller on the reported metrics. Even randomly choosing between useful behaviors benefits from having a capable arm controller underneath. The learned high-level policy performs best overall, using its choices to improve both the modeled energy return and the number of decision steps needed per food item.

This comparison supports the chosen decomposition for this task and training setup. The paper does not establish that every hierarchical method outperforms every end-to-end method, and it does not report further end-to-end benchmarks for the multiarm cases.

With two active arms, the policy can coordinate movement along two orthogonal directions. Four active arms add forward, backward, left, and right movement, making it possible to revisit missed food. In the four-arm experiment without obstacles, the learned policy collects 88% of available food on average, compared with 38% for the greedy policy.

Let contact trigger a local response

An arm reaching toward food can become stuck against an obstacle even when the target is geometrically reachable. We address this with a local reflex inspired by waves of muscle activation observed in octopus arms.

At contact, the part of the arm beyond the contact point relaxes. Toward the base, longitudinal muscles on the contacting side increase activation while the other muscles relax. This reshapes the compliant arm so that it can slide past the obstacle. When contact ends, the original muscle command resumes. The model treats the activation signals as propagating instantaneously.

The four-arm results show both the benefit and its limits:

Evaluation conditionMean fraction of food collected
No obstacles88%
Obstacles, without local reflex21%
Obstacles, with local reflex67%

The high-level policy is trained without obstacles. Adding the reflex at deployment recovers much of the lost performance without retraining that policy, although collection remains below the unobstructed result. The response handles contact locally, allowing the existing foraging decisions to remain useful.

What this teaches us about soft control

The contribution is a way to combine methods with different strengths. Reinforcement learning handles sequences of discrete decisions. A mechanics-based neural controller provides fast reaching commands. Local feedback and physical compliance respond to disturbances where they occur.

These results come from a computational model, with food's horizontal coordinates on a grid compatible with the crawl step, simplified anchoring and collection, and frictionless obstacle contact. They establish a working control strategy in that setting, while hardware performance and more general arm dynamics remain open questions.

For soft robotics, the useful design principle is to make each layer solve a problem it can handle well. A central policy can coordinate a deformable body more effectively when reliable arm behaviors and local responses are already available.

Paper and attribution

This post is based on Hierarchical Control and Learning of a Foraging CyberOctopus, by Chia-Hsien Shih, Noel Naughton, Udit Halder, Heng-Sheng Chang, Seung Hyun Kim, Rhanor Gillette, Prashant G. Mehta, and Mattia Gazzola. The paper appeared in Advanced Intelligent Systems, 5(9), 2300088 (2023), and was first published online on June 22, 2023.

Figures 1, 3, 4, and 7 are reproduced from the published paper, with surrounding page text and original captions removed and explanatory captions supplied here. The article is © 2023 The Authors, published by Wiley-VCH GmbH under CC BY 4.0. The octopus photograph within Figure 1 is separately credited to Anneli Salo under CC BY-SA 3.0.

The paper provides code for multiarm foraging and neural network energy shaping. The BibTeX below cites the published article.

entry.title: Shaping Energy to Control a Muscular Octopus Arm
entry.content:
An octopus arm has no rigid skeleton and no small set of joints to command. It can bend along its length, extend toward an object, and twist to bring its suckers into contact. That flexibility makes the arm a compelling model for soft robots, but it also raises a difficult control question: how should its muscles work together to produce a useful shape?

In our paper, Energy-shaping control of a muscular octopus arm moving in three dimensions, Udit Halder, Chia-Hsien Shih, Noel Naughton, Mattia Gazzola, Prashant G. Mehta, and I approach this problem through energy. We model the arm and its muscles together, then choose muscle activations that make a task-specific shape an equilibrium of the combined system.

The resulting motion comes from the arm's mechanics. Once the activation pattern is applied, elastic forces, muscle forces, inertia, and damping determine how the arm moves toward its new resting configuration. We demonstrate this approach in simulations of reaching and grasping in three dimensions.

Reaching and grasping in motion

Three muscle groups, many possible motions

The geometry of a muscle matters as much as its ability to contract. In an octopus arm, three major muscle groups turn local contraction into different kinds of deformation:

Muscle groupArrangementMain mechanical role
TransverseAcross the arm, surrounding the central nerve cordNarrows the cross-section and extends the arm through approximate volume conservation
LongitudinalAlong the arm, away from its center lineShortens the arm and produces bending when activation is uneven across its sides
ObliqueHelically around the arm, with opposite handednessProduces twisting together with other coupled deformations

We describe the arm as a Cosserat rod. At each location along its center line, the model tracks both a position and the orientation of a small material frame. This lets it describe stretching, shearing, bending, and twisting in one continuum model.

Keeping track of orientation is essential. Two configurations can have similar center lines while presenting different sides of the arm to an object. To model a grasp with the suckers facing inward, we need to control that orientation as well as position.

The implementation uses one transverse activation field, four longitudinal fields, and two oblique fields, one for each handedness. Each field can vary along the arm. The oblique fibers of the same handedness share an activation, giving seven distributed controls overall.

Muscles become part of the energy model

An elastic rod stores energy when it deforms. Its internal forces and bending or twisting moments can be obtained by differentiating that energy with respect to strain. Our key modeling step is to give the muscles a compatible description.

For muscle $m$, the paper constructs a scalar function $W^m$ whose strain derivatives generate its active force and moment. The construction incorporates the muscle's geometry and a force-length relation fitted to experimental data. Multiplying by its activation $u^m$ scales its contribution:

$$ \mathbf n^m=u^m\frac{\partial W^m}{\partial\boldsymbol\nu}, \qquad \mathbf m^m=u^m\frac{\partial W^m}{\partial\boldsymbol\kappa}. $$

Here, $\boldsymbol\nu$ describes shear and stretch, while $\boldsymbol\kappa$ describes bending and twist. The vectors $\mathbf n^m$ and $\mathbf m^m$ are the muscle's internal force and moment in the arm's local frame.

For a fixed spatial activation profile $\alpha^m(s)$, the combined potential energy becomes

$$ V(q;\alpha)=\int_0^L\left[ W^e(\varepsilon(s))+ \sum_m\alpha^m(s)W^m(s,\varepsilon(s)) \right]\,ds. $$

The notation $q$ represents the arm's position and orientation along its length, $\varepsilon=(\boldsymbol\nu,\boldsymbol\kappa)$ collects its strains, and $W^e$ is the passive elastic energy density. The muscle term is written here with its dependence on muscle strain absorbed into $\varepsilon$.

This gives us a family of energy landscapes indexed by muscle activation. It is a mechanical representation of the actuator forces; it does not measure the biological energy consumed by muscle metabolism.

Choose the equilibrium, then let the arm move

The picture at the top of this post captures the control idea. Before activation, a straight arm is at rest in its passive energy landscape. Activating the muscles reshapes that landscape, allowing a bent or twisted configuration to become a new equilibrium.

There is an important constraint: the available muscles determine which landscapes can be produced. A transverse muscle cannot apply an arbitrary sideways force, for example. In conventional energy-shaping design, reconciling a desired energy with these actuator restrictions leads to difficult equations called matching conditions.

Our muscle-energy formulation builds those restrictions into the family $V(q;\alpha)$. We search over physically available activations, with $0\leq\alpha^m(s)\leq1$, to find an equilibrium suited to the task. For the unloaded arm with a fixed base and free tip, the equilibrium condition balances active muscle loads against passive elastic loads.

The search minimizes a combination of activation effort and task error:

$$ J(\alpha,q)= \frac12\sum_m\int_0^L[\alpha^m(s)]^2\,ds +J_{\mathrm{task}}(q). $$

For reaching, the task cost penalizes tip-position and tip-orientation errors. For grasping, it encourages the arm to approach the object and face its suckers toward it, while a penalty discourages penetration. The squared-activation term regularizes muscle effort; minimizing it is not a claim of optimal metabolic efficiency.

The algorithm alternates between three steps:

  1. For the current activations, solve for equilibrium strains and reconstruct the arm from base to tip.
  2. Propagate a costate from tip to base to determine how the task objective responds to changes along the arm.
  3. Update the activations using that information, respecting their bounds, and repeat.

This is an optimal control calculation along the spatial coordinate of the arm. The pose evolves in $SE(3)$, the space of three-dimensional positions and rotations. A useful reduction expresses the costate through two three-component vectors with the interpretation of internal forces and moments.

After optimization, the activation profile is held constant in time. Muscle forces still change as the arm deforms because they depend on its current geometry and muscle lengths. With damping, the model's total mechanical energy is non-increasing along the motion. The paper uses this to argue local asymptotic stability under technical assumptions; a full functional-analytic proof for the infinite-dimensional system is left for future work.

Reaching means getting the orientation right, too

The simulated arm is 20 cm long and tapers from a base radius of 1.2 cm to a tip radius of 0.12 cm. We discretize it into 100 rod elements in Elastica.

In a representative reaching movement, transverse activation extends the distal arm, longitudinal activation near the base bends it toward the target, and oblique activation twists it to orient the suckers. The three muscle groups cooperate to meet a position-and-orientation objective.

We test 125 targets distributed within a cube of side length 20 cm. The largest position errors occur at distant corners outside the arm's reachable workspace. Targets close to the base also challenge the arm's ability to bend and twist at the same time.

The normalized orientation error stays below 0.1 in all tested cases. This is a specific matrix-based measure, $|Q^*-Q(L)|_F^2/8$, rather than an angular error in degrees or a percentage of successful reaches. The experiment shows how the controller performs across a workspace that includes physically difficult and unreachable targets.

Wrapping around an object

Grasping asks more of the arm than bringing its tip to a point. A substantial length of the arm must approach the object, curve around it, and turn its sucker-facing side inward.

We express these requirements through an objective acting on the distal 70% of the arm, together with a non-penetration penalty. Longitudinal and oblique activation then produce a spiral-like configuration around a cylindrical target.

The tests vary cylinder radius from 1 to 4 cm. Thinner cylinders are harder to wrap around: their surfaces require tighter bending, which competes with the activation-effort penalty. Separate tests keep the radius at 2 cm and vary the cylinder's tilt from $-60^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ about each of two axes.

Across those tilt tests, the position-error measure varies less than the orientation-error measure. The chosen objective places greater weight on proximity, so keeping the arm close to the cylinder can take priority over perfectly orienting the suckers.

Here, grasping means achieving the wrapping configuration in simulation. Sucker adhesion and sensing are outside this model, and the experiments do not test holding or lifting a load.

What energy shaping gives us

The contribution is a connection between anatomy, mechanics, and control design. Muscle geometry determines forces and moments; a common energy description combines them with elasticity; optimization selects activations for a useful equilibrium. The arm's dynamics then produce the transition toward that configuration.

This provides a way to coordinate a highly deformable body without prescribing the full motion of every point along it. It also keeps the actuator constraints visible throughout the design.

The demonstrated tasks involve static targets and a simulated arm. Extending the approach to moving targets, sensory feedback, and neural control requires additional work. Still, the study gives a concrete starting point for soft robotic manipulation: design how the body wants to settle, and use its mechanics to help it get there.

Paper and attribution

This post is based on Energy-shaping control of a muscular octopus arm moving in three dimensions, by Heng-Sheng Chang, Udit Halder, Chia-Hsien Shih, Noel Naughton, Mattia Gazzola, and Prashant G. Mehta. The paper appeared in Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 479(2270), 20220593 (2023).

The technical discussion and Figures 2, 3, 5, and 6 follow the arXiv:2209.04089v1 preprint, submitted September 9, 2022.
